docs.title: E — Analysis
docs.text:
1. Why does the optimizer choose to pay more KL?

At initialization the encoder outputs \(\mu \approx \mathbf{0}\) and \(\log\sigma^2 \approx \mathbf{0}\) for every image, so \(q(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{x}) \approx \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})\): the KL is essentially zero (0.03 nats on validation before the first step) but \(\mathbf{z}\) carries no information about \(\mathbf{x}\), and the reconstruction costs 544.7 nats. The KL is the price of information: it measures how far, in nats, each image's posterior moves away from the prior — how much \(\mathbf{z}\) tells about which image it came from. The decoder can only reconstruct a specific digit if \(\mathbf{z}\) says which one, so every nat of KL the encoder spends buys a reduction in reconstruction. As long as one more nat of KL saves more than one nat of reconstruction, the total \(L = \text{rec} + \text{KL}\) goes down, and gradient descent takes the deal. Figure 1 shows the exchange rate: on train, from epoch 2 to epoch 20, the KL rises by 5.1 nats (14.50 → 19.57) while the reconstruction falls by 36.6 (117.78 → 81.19); measured from the untrained model, about 19.5 nats of KL bought about 460 nats of reconstruction. The KL flattens near 19.5 when the next nat of information no longer pays for itself.

The trade is visible dimension by dimension: on the training set, 11 of the 16 latent dimensions are used (variance of \(\mu_i\) across images ≈ 0.86–1.10, posterior std \(\sigma_i \approx 0.09\)–0.40), while the other 5 have \(\mu_i \approx 0\) for every image and \(\sigma_i \approx 1\) — exactly the prior, zero KL, zero information. The optimizer pays KL only in the dimensions where the information is worth more than it costs, and switches the rest off.

2. Why do the samples (Figure 3) look worse than the reconstructions (Figure 2)?

(a) Where prior samples land. The prior asks the aggregate of all posteriors to look like \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})\), but with \(\beta = 1\) the KL is only a soft penalty: each training image occupies a small Gaussian blob (\(\sigma_i \approx 0.1\)–0.4 in the active dimensions) and the union of 50 000 blobs in 11 active dimensions does not fill the whole prior — it leaves holes and low-density regions between digit classes. A \(\mathbf{z}\) drawn from the prior can land there, where the decoder was (almost) never trained, and it decodes to something that is not a digit, or a blend of two (row 2 column 5, row 3 column 8, row 6 column 8 in Figure 3). In numbers: the median distance from a prior sample to the nearest training \(\mu\) is 2.58, while for a test image's \(\mu\) it is 1.08 — prior samples land, on average, much farther from anything the decoder learned on than real encodings do. A reconstruction never has this problem: \(\mu\) of a real image is by construction in a region the decoder trained on.

(b) What the decoder outputs for a given \(\mathbf{z}\). The decoder does not output an image; it outputs the Bernoulli probabilities \(\hat x_j = p(x_j = 1\mid\mathbf{z})\), i.e. the mean \(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}\mid\mathbf{z}]\). Many training images (different stroke widths, small shifts) map to overlapping neighbourhoods of the latent space, and the BCE-optimal output for that \(\mathbf{z}\) is their pixel-wise average — so pixels where the strokes disagree come out grey, and we display that mean instead of sampling binary pixels from it. This affects reconstructions too (Figure 2: 14.6% of decoded pixels are grey, between 0.1 and 0.9, against 8.6% in the real test images), but it is worse for prior samples (16.8%) because in the poorly-covered regions of (a) the decoder's uncertainty, and so the averaging, is larger.

3. Why decode \(\mu\) rather than a sampled \(\mathbf{z}\) in Figure 2?

\(\mu\) is the encoder's best guess for the code of that image — the centre of \(q(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{x})\), its most probable point. A sampled \(\mathbf{z} = \mu + \sigma\odot\varepsilon\) adds noise that is useful during training (it forces nearby codes to decode to similar images, which is what makes the latent space smooth), but at display time it would only make the figure random: a different \(\varepsilon\) gives a slightly different reconstruction, and in the 5 inactive dimensions \(\sigma \approx 1\), so a sample would wander in directions that carry nothing. Decoding \(\mu\) gives a deterministic, reproducible picture of what the model has learned about that image.

The grid points are \(z = \Phi^{-1}(q)\) with \(q \in \{0.05, 0.114, \dots, 0.95\}\) (15 values), i.e. \(z \in \{-1.645, -1.204, -0.921, \dots, 0, \dots, 1.204, 1.645\}\), in both coordinates. Why this spacing: since \(\Phi\) is the CDF of the prior, consecutive points \(\Phi^{-1}(q_k)\) and \(\Phi^{-1}(q_{k+1})\) always enclose the same prior probability \(q_{k+1} - q_k\), so every cell of the grid holds the same prior mass — the grid is dense near the origin, where most of the prior (and of the data) is, and sparse in the tails, instead of wasting cells on regions the prior almost never samples.

docs.title: E — Analysis
docs.text:
1. Which digits overlap in Figure 4, and what does the transition look like in Figure 5?

The clearest overlap is 4 and 9: in Figure 4 the purple (4) and cyan (9) clouds sit on top of each other around \(\mu \approx (0.7, 0)\) to \((0.9, 0.1)\) (class centroids \((0.73, 0.00)\) and \((0.88, 0.06)\)). A 15-nearest-neighbour classifier fit on the training \(\mu\)'s reaches 82.2% on the test \(\mu\)'s, and its most frequent confusion is 4 ↔ 9 (572 of the test errors), followed by 5 ↔ 8 (263), 3 ↔ 5 (154), 3 ↔ 8 (136) and 7 ↔ 9 (120). The 3, 5 and 8 clouds are the second overlap: they share the centre of the plane (centroids \((-0.68, -0.21)\), \((-0.31, 0.02)\), \((-0.41, 0.11)\)).

In Figure 5 the 4 ↔ 9 transition is in the right half, columns \(z_1 \approx 0.16\) to \(0.92\), rows \(z_2 \approx -0.5\) to \(0.7\): going from the "4"s to the "9"s, the open top of the 4 gradually closes — the two upper strokes bend towards each other and merge into a loop — and the in-between cells are a 4 with an almost-closed head, which is exactly the ambiguous handwriting that makes these classes overlap. The 3/5/8 overlap is the centre-left of the grid (\(z_1 \approx -0.9\) to \(0\), \(z_2 \approx 0\) to \(0.7\)): an 8 whose upper-left part fades into a 5, and a 3 whose left side closes into an 8; the in-between images are blurrier and fainter than the pure digits, because the decoder averages the classes it cannot separate there.

2. What do two numbers per image force the model to discard?

With two numbers the code has room for little more than which digit and one or two coarse style factors. Figure 5 is the evidence: across the whole plane the only variations are the class, a slant (the 1s go from tilted to upright from left to right in the top rows) and a bit of width (the 0s in the bottom row get rounder from left to right). Everything else that distinguishes one handwritten digit from another — stroke thickness, the exact length and position of each stroke, small loops, gaps, serifs, an unusual shape — has no coordinate to live in, so the decoder outputs a prototypical digit of the class plus a slant, and every individual detail is paid for in reconstruction. That is the 51.7-nat gap. It is largest for digits with the most individual variation in shape and smallest for the simplest: decoding \(\mu\), the test reconstruction of a 2 goes from 92.2 (\(d = 16\)) to 166.0 (\(d = 2\)), of an 8 from 96.9 to 161.9, of a 3 from 87.4 to 151.5, while a 1 — one straight stroke, fully described by its slant — only goes from 35.9 to 52.2. The KL tells the same story: the \(d = 2\) model can only spend 6.8 nats of information per image, against 19.5 for \(d = 16\).

3. Pixel-space vs. latent-space interpolation (Figure 6).

The latent row is the one that passes through digit-like images. It is one object that changes shape: the "1" first bends into a curved stroke (\(t = 0.22\)–\(0.33\)), then the stroke opens into a narrow loop (\(t \approx 0.44\)–\(0.56\) — the least clean frames, a thin "0"/"8"-like shape) that widens into the "0". The amount of ink also follows the shape, not a straight line: it stays near the 1's (39 → 50 pixels of ink) until \(t = 0.33\) and only then grows to the 0's 145. The pixel row never looks like a digit: every intermediate frame is the "1" and the "0" superimposed, each at partial intensity — a faded loop with a vertical bar through it, the ink growing linearly from 39 to 145. Measured by the RMS distance to the nearest of the 50 000 training images, the pixel midpoint (\(t = 0.56\)) is 0.198 away, the latent one 0.168; the pixel row is farther from real digits at every intermediate step.

The reason: the set of images of handwritten digits is a thin, curved surface in the 784-dimensional pixel space. The average of two points on it is a point off it — superimposing two digits is not a digit. The VAE's latent space is trained so that nearby codes decode to similar images and (through the KL) codes are packed together around the origin, so the straight segment between \(\mu_a\) and \(\mu_b\) stays mostly in regions the decoder learned, and every point on it is mapped back onto the surface of digit-like images. It is not perfect: the middle of the segment crosses the space between the "1" and "0" clusters, which is less populated (the same holes as in 1E.2a), and those frames are the blurriest of the row.

docs.text:
def load_raw(path=DATA_PATH):
    """The CSV as published (agent/company 'NULL' strings are read as NaN)."""
    return pd.read_csv(path)


def clean(df):
    """Row-level rules that need no statistic from the data (safe to apply before the split).

    1. exact duplicate rows are dropped (no booking ID exists to tell them apart; kept, the
       same row would land in train and in test);
    2. bookings with 0 guests (adults + children + babies = 0) are invalid records;
    3. has_company = 1 if a company paid / booked (company is 94% missing).
    """
    df = df.drop_duplicates().copy()
    guests = df["adults"] + df["children"].fillna(0) + df["babies"]
    df = df[guests > 0].copy()
    df["has_company"] = df["company"].notna().astype(int)
    df["agent"] = df["agent"].astype("Int64").astype(str).replace("<NA>", np.nan)
    return df.reset_index(drop=True)


def split(df, test_size=0.2):
    """Stratified 80/20 split with a fixed seed. Returns X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test."""
    X, y = df.drop(columns=[TARGET]), df[TARGET]
    return train_test_split(X, y, test_size=test_size, stratify=y, random_state=SEED)


def load_clean_split():
    """Raw CSV -> clean rows -> stratified split -> model features only."""
    X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = split(clean(load_raw()))
    return X_train[FEATURES], X_test[FEATURES], y_train, y_test

df = P.clean(raw)                                 # duplicates + 0-guest rows removed
X_train_all, X_test_all, y_train, y_test = P.split(df)   # stratified 80/20, random_state=42
train = X_train_all.assign(**{P.TARGET: y_train})  # all analysis below: TRAINING SET ONLY
  • Only two row rules come before the split, and neither uses a statistic of the data: drop exact duplicates and drop 0-guest bookings. No other decision has been made yet.
  • Split 80 / 20, stratified by the target, random_state = 42: 69 784 train / 17 446 test, 27.52% canceled in both.
  • Why stratified and not temporal: the cancellation rate is stable over the years (37.0%, 35.9%, 38.7% for 2015, 2016, 2017 in the raw file), but it is strongly seasonal (14% to 34% by month and hotel, Figure 9). The data cover only 26 months, so a temporal split (last 20% of arrivals ≈ May–August 2017) would test on summer only, mixing "can the model predict cancellations" with "does it transfer to another season". The year is dropped from the features so the model cannot lean on it.
  • From here on, every statistic is computed on the training set only — the test set is not looked at again until the pipeline is applied to it in 4.C.

Spearman, not Pearson. Most numerical features are skewed, zero-inflated or ordinal counts (Table 3), and a single extreme value (adr = 5 400, adults = 50) can dominate a Pearson coefficient. The difference is visible: previous_bookings_not_canceled × is_repeated_guest has Pearson 0.443 but Spearman 0.805 (Table 6). For this analysis the month is also converted to its number (1–12).

docs.text:
Each choice points to the finding that motivates it; every statistic (median, quantile, mean, standard deviation, list of categories) is learned with fit on the training set only.

Missing values (training set: children 3, country 364, agent 9 733 rows; Table 2).

  • children → median (0): 3 rows (< 0.01%), and 90% of the bookings have 0 children (Table 3).
  • country and agent → constant category "missing": for agent, missing means "booked without a travel agency" (14% of the rows, Table 5), which is information; for country (0.5%) it keeps the row without inventing a country.
  • company → dropped and replaced by the flag has_company (94.3% missing, section 1.B).

Outliers — clip each numerical feature to [0, 99.9th percentile of the training set] (UpperClipper), then log1p where the rule below says so. Motivated by Table 3: the maxima are far from the bulk (adr 5 400 € vs Q3 134 €, adults 50 vs Q3 2, days_in_waiting_list 391 vs 99% zeros), and one negative adr. Clipping instead of dropping rows, because a deployed model must also score unusual bookings, and because without it the 5 400 € booking would sit about 95 standard deviations from the mean after scaling — a single input able to saturate the network's activations. Rows affected: 599 training bookings (0.86%) have at least one clipped value.

Categorical encoding — one-hot (OneHotEncoder), because no categorical feature has a usable order for a network (room codes are anonymised; months are cyclic, and a 1–12 number would put December far from January). Two findings shape the encoder:

  • high cardinality and rare categories (Figure 5, Table 5) → min_frequency = 50: categories with fewer than 50 training bookings are merged into one infrequent column per feature. country becomes 48 columns instead of 170 and agent 81 instead of 316, keeping 98.2% / 96.2% of their rows in their own column;

Scaling — StandardScaler on the numerical features (after clip/log), because their ranges go from 0–4 (total_of_special_requests) and 0–3 (adults, clipped) to 0–484 (lead_time, clipped) and 0–337 € (adr, clipped) (Table 3/Table 4). For a network trained by gradient descent, inputs on such different scales give some weights gradients orders of magnitude larger than others; standardised inputs (mean 0, std 1) also keep tanh/sigmoid units out of saturation. The 0/1 flags and one-hot columns are left as they are (already in [0, 1]). After the fit, the largest |mean| of a scaled column is 0.000 on train and 0.013 on test — the test set is transformed with the training statistics, as it should.

docs.text:
All projections use the 192 preprocessed training columns (output of 4.C), coloured by the target. PCA is fitted on the whole training set; t-SNE and UMAP, which are slow and quadratic in memory, on a stratified sample of 5 000 training bookings (27.5% canceled, as the full set).

Figure 12 — PCA: cumulative explained variance (log x-axis), the sample projected on PC1–PC2, and the largest loadings of PC1 and PC2.

PCA. PC1 explains 12.9% and PC2 8.2% — 21.2% together; 16 components are needed for 80% and 40 for 95% of the variance. The variance is spread over many directions: the 192 columns are mostly independent one-hot indicators. Reading the loadings:

  • PC1 — "size of the booking" vs "loyal customer": positive on lead_time (0.41), adults (0.39), stays_in_week_nights (0.36), adr (0.35) and stays_in_weekend_nights (0.30); negative on previous_bookings_not_canceled (−0.35) and previous_cancellations (−0.21). High PC1 = a first-time customer booking a long, expensive stay for more people, well in advance.
  • PC2 — "long cheap stay" vs "short expensive family stay": positive on the two stay lengths (0.43, 0.42) and lead_time (0.33), negative on adr (−0.41), children (−0.28) and total_of_special_requests (−0.21).

Both components are made of the 13 standardised numerical columns: a one-hot column has variance p(1−p) ≤ 0.25, against 1 for a standardised feature, so PCA on this mixed matrix is dominated by the numerical part. Also, the last 10 of the 192 components have exactly zero variance: inside each of the 10 one-hot blocks the columns sum to 1, so each block adds one exact linear dependency (the "dummy-variable trap"). It is harmless for PCA and for a network with regularisation, but it means the matrix has only 182 independent directions. In the PC1–PC2 plane the classes overlap almost completely.

import umap  # noqa: E402

PERPLEXITIES, NEIGHBORS = (10, 30, 100), (5, 15, 100)   # 3 values each, to look for what is stable
emb = {}
for perp in PERPLEXITIES:
    emb[f"tsne_{perp}"] = TSNE(n_components=2, perplexity=perp, init="pca", random_state=SEED
                               ).fit_transform(Xs)
for nn in NEIGHBORS:
    emb[f"umap_{nn}"] = umap.UMAP(n_neighbors=nn, min_dist=0.1, random_state=SEED
                                  ).fit_transform(Xs)

Figure 13 — t-SNE of the 5 000-booking sample, perplexity 10, 30 and 100.

Figure 14 — UMAP of the same sample, n_neighbors 5, 15 and 100 (min_dist = 0.1).

What the islands are. To read the nonlinear maps instead of guessing, DBSCAN was run on the 2-D UMAP (n_neighbors = 15) map and each group described by its cancellation rate and the features shared by its members:

Table 7 — Groups found by DBSCAN (eps = 0.6, min_samples = 20) on the UMAP map with n_neighbors = 15; 33 points are left as noise.

(Full table, with every descriptor, in figures/tables.txt, section t7.) The islands are the rare non-zero values of zero-inflated features: after log1p + standardisation, a single non-zero value puts a booking several standard deviations away from the 95–99% of zeros, so it forms its own neighbourhood. The first version of this analysis had one more island — 409 bookings, 0% canceled, all with required_car_parking_spaces > 0 — which is how the parking leak of section 1.B was found.

Evaluating the maps, and a control. A map can look clustered without saying anything about the data, so each map is measured on two separate questions, and the same procedure is run on a control: the sample with every column shuffled independently (each feature keeps its distribution, but the relations between features and with the target are destroyed).

from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN  # noqa: E402
from sklearn.manifold import trustworthiness  # noqa: E402
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score  # noqa: E402
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score  # noqa: E402
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier  # noqa: E402


def evaluate_map(X_high, Z):
    """Two separate questions about a 2-D map Z of X_high:
    - is the neighbourhood preserved?  trustworthiness at k = 5 (local) and k = 30 (wider), in [0, 1]
    - is the TARGET separated?         silhouette with the target labels, and 15-NN accuracy (5-fold CV)
    plus the number of groups DBSCAN finds on the standardised map (how 'clustered' it looks)."""
    Zs = (Z - Z.mean(0)) / Z.std(0)
    return {"trust_k5": r(trustworthiness(X_high, Z, n_neighbors=5)),
            "trust_k30": r(trustworthiness(X_high, Z, n_neighbors=30)),
            "silhouette_target": r(silhouette_score(Z, ys)),
            "knn15_acc": r(cross_val_score(KNeighborsClassifier(15), Z, ys, cv=5).mean()),
            "dbscan_groups": int(len(set(DBSCAN(eps=0.15, min_samples=20).fit_predict(Zs)) - {-1}))}


evals = {name: evaluate_map(Xs, Z) for name, Z in [("PCA (2 PCs)", Z_pca)] + list(emb.items())}

# Control: shuffle every column independently. Each feature keeps its distribution (same zeros,
# same tails) but the relations between features — and with the target — are destroyed.
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
Xs_shuffled = np.column_stack([rng.permutation(col) for col in Xs.T])
control = {"tsne_30 (shuffled)": TSNE(n_components=2, perplexity=30, init="pca", random_state=SEED
                                      ).fit_transform(Xs_shuffled),
           "umap_15 (shuffled)": umap.UMAP(n_neighbors=15, min_dist=0.1, random_state=SEED
                                           ).fit_transform(Xs_shuffled)}
evals.update({name: evaluate_map(Xs_shuffled, Z) for name, Z in control.items()})

# Can the map place NEW bookings (e.g. the test set)? PCA and UMAP learn a mapping; t-SNE does not.
has_transform = {"PCA": hasattr(pca, "transform"), "UMAP": hasattr(umap.UMAP(), "transform"),
                 "t-SNE": hasattr(TSNE(), "transform")}

Table 9 — Every 2-D map of the 5 000-booking sample: trustworthiness (are the neighbours in the map neighbours in the 192-D space? 1 = perfect) at k = 5 and k = 30; separation of the target (silhouette with the target labels, and 15-NN accuracy, 5-fold CV); and the number of groups DBSCAN finds. Reference: the majority class gives 0.725 accuracy, a 15-NN on the full 192 columns 0.787.

Figure 15 — Control: t-SNE (perplexity 30) and UMAP (n_neighbors 15) of the same sample after shuffling every column independently.

Comparison of the three methods.

  • Neighbourhoods: t-SNE (trustworthiness 0.988–0.991 at k = 5) and UMAP (0.949–0.972) keep the local neighbours; PCA does not (0.750). PCA keeps the directions of largest global variance, which here are the numerical features, and squashes everything that differs by one-hot indicators on top of each other.
  • What the nonlinear maps reveal that PCA does not: sub-populations with very different cancellation rates (Table 7: past cancellers 70%, loyal customers 4%, Direct bookings 13%) that PCA mixes in one cloud. The target is better separated in the nonlinear maps: 15-NN accuracy 0.750–0.767 against 0.705 for PCA, below even the majority class (0.725).
  • The control changes how the islands must be read. The shuffled data also form 7–9 DBSCAN groups with trustworthiness 0.91–0.98 (Figure 15): the number of islands is produced by the distributions of the features alone — zero-inflated counts and one-hot columns, where a single non-zero value puts a booking far from all the zeros. So the existence of islands is not evidence of structure. What the real maps have and the control does not is the relation with the target: 15-NN accuracy 0.760 (t-SNE 30) and 0.762 (UMAP 15) vs 0.714 and 0.711 on shuffled data (no better than the majority class), and silhouette with the target 0.013–0.040 vs −0.006/−0.008. The reading of Table 7 is therefore about which bookings fall together and their cancellation rates, which the control does not reproduce, not about how many islands there are.
  • Effect of the parameters (3 values each): small perplexity / n_neighbors keep the closest neighbours best (t-SNE trustworthiness at k = 5: 0.991 → 0.988; UMAP: 0.972 → 0.949) and fragment the data into more groups (t-SNE 9 → 7 → 5, UMAP 8 → 8 → 7 DBSCAN groups); large values give fewer, bigger groups and a more global layout. Table 10 checks which groups survive every value: a group made 100% of bookings with children, with babies, or on the waiting list appears in all six maps; the previous-cancellations group in 5 of 6 (it merges into a larger group with t-SNE perplexity 100); repeated guests form a ~80%-pure group in 5 of 6. Those are the stable findings; the rest of the layout changes with the parameter. The separation of the target barely moves (0.750–0.767), so no parameter value "reveals" the classes: it is not a reason to choose one. | | previous_cancellations | children | babies | days_in_waiting_list | is_repeated_guest | |:---------|-------------------------:|-----------:|---------:|-----------------------:|--------------------:| | tsne_10 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 0.88 | | tsne_30 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 0.82 | | tsne_100 | 0.02 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 0.04 | | umap_5 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 0.83 | | umap_15 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 0.81 | | umap_100 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 0.83 |

Table 10 — Stability across parameters: for each map and each rare non-zero value, the share of bookings with that value in the most homogeneous DBSCAN group (1.00 = some group is made only of those bookings).

  • Limits: the sizes of the islands and the distances between them have no direct meaning in t-SNE or UMAP, so the reading above only uses which points are together. And t-SNE cannot place new data: it has no transform (has_transform = PCA True, UMAP True, t-SNE False), so it can only be used to explore the training set, never inside a model or to project the test set. PCA and UMAP learn a mapping that can be applied to new bookings. No 2-D map separates the classes: the decision needs many features at once, which is the job of the network.

docs.text:
class UpperClipper(BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin):
    """Clip each column to [lower, q-quantile of the TRAINING data]."""

    def __init__(self, q=CLIP_Q, lower=0.0):
        self.q, self.lower = q, lower

    def fit(self, X, y=None):
        self.upper_ = np.nanquantile(np.asarray(X, dtype=float), self.q, axis=0)
        return self

    def transform(self, X):
        return np.clip(np.asarray(X, dtype=float), self.lower, self.upper_)

    def get_feature_names_out(self, input_features=None):
        return np.asarray(input_features, dtype=object)


def build_preprocessor():
    """ColumnTransformer that turns the raw features into a dense, NaN-free, scaled matrix."""
    num_log = Pipeline([
        ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),          # children: 4 NaN
        ("clip", UpperClipper()),                               # extreme tails (q 0.999)
        ("log", FunctionTransformer(np.log1p, feature_names_out="one-to-one")),
        ("scale", StandardScaler()),
    ])
    num_lin = Pipeline([
        ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
        ("clip", UpperClipper()),                               # adr < 0 -> 0, adults up to 50
        ("scale", StandardScaler()),
    ])
    cat = Pipeline([
        ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="constant", fill_value="missing")),  # country, agent
        ("onehot", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist",
                                 min_frequency=MIN_FREQ, sparse_output=False)),
    ])
    return ColumnTransformer([
        ("num_log", num_log, NUM_LOG),
        ("num_lin", num_lin, NUM_LIN),
        ("bin", "passthrough", BINARY),
        ("cat", cat, CATEGORICAL),
    ], verbose_feature_names_out=True)

pre = P.build_preprocessor()
Xt_train = pre.fit_transform(X_train)        # every statistic (median, q99.9, mean/std, categories)
Xt_test = pre.transform(X_test)              # ... is learned on X_train and only applied to X_test
names = pre.get_feature_names_out()
print("NaN train/test:", np.isnan(Xt_train).sum(), np.isnan(Xt_test).sum())
print("shape train/test:", Xt_train.shape, Xt_test.shape)

docs.title: 5. Synthesis
docs.text:
Main findings (for whoever builds the model):

  1. Four columns leak the target and are removed: reservation_status, reservation_status_date, assigned_room_type, required_car_parking_spaces (section 1.B; 100%, 100%, 5.4% vs 41.6% and 0% evidence).
  2. 26.8% of the file are exact duplicates, mostly non-refundable group bookings; removing them takes the cancellation rate from 37.0% to 27.5% (Figure 1).
  3. Strongest single signals: deposit_type = Non Refund (95.0% canceled), previous_cancellations > 0 (66.1% canceled, 1 367 training bookings), long lead_time (median 80 vs 38 days, Figure 10), the channel (Online TA 35.3% vs Direct 14.9%) and the country (Portugal 35.8% vs ~19%) (Figures 8–9).
  4. Hotel × month interactions in both the cancellation rate and the price (Figures 9 and 11).
  5. Feature shapes: zero-inflated counts and two long-tail categorical features (Figures 2, 3, 5), handled by clipping + log1p + standardisation and one-hot with an infrequent bucket.
  6. No 2-D view separates the classes (Figures 12–15, Table 9): the best 2-D map keeps 76.7% 15-NN accuracy vs 72.5% for the majority class (78.7% on the full 192 columns), and the shuffled control shows that the islands of t-SNE / UMAP come from the shape of the features, not from groups of bookings.
